entries.longDescription:
The American mission came to Syria hoping to reform the old churches, not to found a new one. Pliny Fisk reached Beirut on 10 July 1823. Henry Jessup wrote the mission's history in 1910. He says the mission board hoped that the heads of the Eastern churches could be led to reform them. Instead, he says, the missionaries were cursed and reviled, and Bibles and tracts were burned.

In 1835 the missionaries ruled that they would not seek members from the native churches. But they would not refuse the sacraments to a member who asked for them. Converts then asked for a church of their own. Jessup says the first Protestant Native Syrian Church was organized in 1848. He writes as a partisan, and he calls the attempt to reform the old churches a failure. The Eastern churches' own side is not told in anything read here.

The missionaries also made a new Arabic Bible. Eli Smith began it in 1848. Butrus el Bistany made a first text from the Hebrew and Greek. Sheikh Nasif el Yazigy knew only Arabic. He rewrote it and sifted out foreign idioms. Dr. Van Dyck reported the Old Testament finished on 22 August 1864. On Friday 10 March 1865 the missionaries held a celebration at the American Press for the printed book.

Egypt had its own mission. Andrew Watson, who served in it, wrote its history in 1897. Thomas McCague and James Barnett began work in Cairo in 1854. On 15 February 1863 the converts there formed the first native congregation. It chose four elders and three deacons.

Some converts came from the Coptic Church. Watson names Wasif Khayat of Asyut, who had dared to join the Evangelical church. The patriarch offered to win him the title of bey if he would return to the Coptic Church. In 1867, Watson writes, the viceroy and the patriarchate united to root out the Protestants and drive the missionaries out of Egypt. In one report he prints, the patriarch, at Asyut, had the priest of Beni Aleig beaten and removed from his priesthood. The priest had let his brother, a Protestant student, hold evangelistic services in his church after Mass.

No Coptic voice on these events is read here, and no Arabic text from the churches themselves.
voices: Pliny Fisk — the American missionary who reached Beirut on 10 July 1823, remembered by Jessup as the pioneer missionary of Beirut
Butrus el Bistany and Sheikh Nasif el Yazigy — the two Arab scholars who worked with the American missionaries on the Arabic Bible
Asaad es Shidiak — an Arab convert whom Jessup calls the first convert and the proto-martyr of modern Syria
entries.legacy: Jessup says that by his time twenty-eight more churches had been organized in the Syria mission. Watson counts 248,386 volumes of Scripture given out by the Egypt mission between 1854 and 1896. Whether these churches carry on today is not shown by any dated source read here.

entries.informalName: The Moravians in the world mission
entries.region: Jamaica, Cape Colony, Suriname, Labrador, Nyasa, Germany
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). It carries the Moravian Church on from 1815, where the entry on Herrnhut stops. Its window runs from 1815 to 1906.
entries.sourcing: Rich for the missions, and told from the Moravian side. J. Taylor Hamilton's history of 1901 is by a member of the church's own executive board. The converts speak only as the missionaries report them. Nothing Moravian after 1815 is yet held in the Library.
entries.floorNote: No question. It is the same church as the entry on Herrnhut.
entries.relationsSummary: This is the same church as the one at Herrnhut, carried on past 1815. In Jamaica its congregations stood beside the Baptist and Wesleyan churches, which have an entry of their own. After the rising of 1831, missionaries of all three were arrested or tried, and none was convicted.
entries.why: When the British law ending slavery took effect on 1 August 1834, the Moravian chapels of Jamaica filled. The church's own historian, J. Taylor Hamilton, wrote that 'The thankful people thronged the churches'. Full freedom waited four more years, for the law first bound the freed to an apprenticeship. The Moravians had been in the West Indies for a century by then. After 1815 they carried the same mission on in the Cape, in Suriname, in Labrador and, from the early 1890s, north of Lake Nyasa.
entries.teaser: Moravian missions, 1815 to 1906. On 1 August 1834 the chapels of Jamaica filled. A first baptism came by an African lake.

sources.work: J. Taylor Hamilton, A History of the Missions of the Moravian Church during the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries (Bethlehem, Pa.: Times Publishing Co., 1901)

entries.longDescription:
The Moravian Church did not stop in 1815. Its mission fields went on, and new ones opened. J. Taylor Hamilton wrote its mission history in 1901. He sat on the church's executive board and taught at its seminary. His book covers the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries in one account.

In Jamaica the church ran twenty-six schools by March 1834. On 1 August 1834 a law of Parliament ended slavery throughout the British colonies. Hamilton notes that an apprenticeship of four or six years came first. He says the freed crowds spent Emancipation Day 'in a manner worthy of its significance'. By the end of 1835 the church had 8,521 members on the island. That was 1,339 more than a year before.

At the Cape the Moravian mission began again in 1792. Hamilton says it had 2,386 members when slavery was ended there on 1 December 1834. The slaves of the colony were fully free on 1 December 1838. In the year after that, Genadendal alone took in four hundred and fifty people. Each case was decided on its own merits.

In Suriname slavery ended by royal proclamation on 1 July 1863. Hamilton says about two-thirds of all the slaves had already been in touch with the Moravian Church. By 1869 he counts 24,330 members in the colony.

In Labrador the winter of 1836 to 1837 brought a famine. Its misery was worst, Hamilton says, at Nain, Okak and Hebron. The church at Hebron was dedicated in October 1837.

Hamilton dates the Nyasa mission to 1890 in one passage and to 1891 in another. Four missionaries went to the country north of Lake Nyasa, and they founded Rungwe among the Konde people. On 7 February 1897 a woman named Fiabarema stood up after a farewell sermon at Rungwe. She said, 'I have risen to say that I belong to God.' She was baptized that evening. Within nine years the church manned four stations there and counted more than one hundred converts.
voices: J. Taylor Hamilton — the church's own historian of its missions, writing in 1901 as a member of its executive board
Fiabarema — the woman at Rungwe, by Lake Nyasa, who rose after a sermon on 7 February 1897 to say she belonged to God, as the missionary's account reports her
entries.legacy: Hamilton closes his account at the end of the nineteenth century. The church's later story is not told here. The entry on Herrnhut says most Moravians now live in Tanzania and the Caribbean. No dated count of today is read here, so that claim is not tested.

set.longDescription:
In 1722 a handful of families slipped over the Bohemian border into Saxony. They were the remnant of the Unity of the Brethren, the Czech reform church. It had survived in hiding for nearly a century after the Habsburgs outlawed it. Count Nikolaus von Zinzendorf let them settle on his estate, and they built a village called Herrnhut. Years of quarreling followed, among the refugees and the other seekers who joined them. Then on 13 August 1727 they shared the Lord's Supper, and they always dated their renewal from that day. What followed was remarkable for a settlement of a few hundred people. They kept a prayer watch in shifts around the clock. They sorted the church into 'choirs' by age and state of life. They wrote up a diary every single day, and thousands of ordinary members set down their own life stories. From 1732 they sent missionaries to the enslaved people of St Thomas, and to Greenland and Suriname. Others went to the Native congregations of Pennsylvania and New York. They were not the first, for Lutherans trained at Halle had reached India in 1706.

The Brethren tried the Cape early. George Schmidt landed there on 9 July 1737. He taught Khoikhoi children to read, and he baptized seven people. The Brethren had to leave in 1745. In 1786 some of them met a woman Schmidt had baptized, and she still prized the Dutch Bible he had given her. The Herrnhut synod of 1789 renewed the plan. Three missionaries reached the Cape on 21 November 1792.

The Brethren also looked to North Africa. La Trobe wrote in 1771 that three Brethren lived at Cairo, with the Copts of Egypt and Abyssinia as their special aim. In 1752 Dr. Frederick William Hooker went to Cairo, on the way to the Christians of Abyssinia. Watson's history says he met the Coptic patriarch, who gave him a letter in reply to one from Count Zinzendorf. In Algiers, Brother Richter went in 1740 to the Christian slaves. He died of the plague. Another Brother stayed there from 1744 to 1748.

Not every Czech Protestant had left. In 1781 the emperor Joseph II issued a Patent of Toleration. It freed the Lutherans and Calvinists. It left out even the Unity of the Brethren. Count Lützow wrote in 1920 that many Bohemians had secretly stayed Protestant. They were glad of the Patent. The Toleration churches after 1781 are not told here.

set.longDescription:
After 1650 the heirs of the Swiss and Dutch Anabaptists lived on as settled churches. Many were called Mennonites, after Menno Simons. Their Dordrecht Confession of 1632 stayed their rule of faith. In 1660 Thieleman van Braght of Dordrecht published the Martyrs Mirror. It told of those "Who Baptized Only Upon Confession of Faith". In a prayer dated at Dort in 1659, he asked to be like "my slain fellow brethren and sisters".

In Pennsylvania the Mennonites wanted their great martyr book in German, not Dutch. The Ephrata community in Lancaster County did the work. Fifteen of its brothers were set to it, and the job took three years. The edition ran to 1300 copies.

The old hymn book of the Swiss Brethren, the Ausbund, was printed again and again in Pennsylvania. Its songs, the title says, were written in the prison at Passau. A Lancaster printing of 1856 calls itself the seventh in Pennsylvania. In 1886 Mennonite publishers brought out the Martyrs Mirror in English. English was spreading "year by year" among "our Mennonite people", its preface says.

In 1890 a manual from Elkhart set out the church's forms. A minister was chosen by lot. A slip with a verse from Proverbs went into one of several like books. The man whose book held it was ordained. Some congregations, "especially among the Amish and Russian Mennonites", chose by the members' vote instead.

The Mennonites also had a Russian chapter. Gerhard Wiebe, an elder of Bergthal, told it in 1900. A call came from Russia, he writes, and the first families left Prussia in 1788 or 1789. By 1790 eight villages had been settled. In the Molotschna colony thirty-nine villages were settled between 1804 and 1824. In the early 1870s the Mennonites read in the newspapers that they would be drafted. They sent men to St Petersburg. Many then left for America. Wiebe says his last brethren came from Russia in 1876.

The Hutterites, a church of their own, have a Russian chapter too. Josef Beck, who edited their chronicles, wrote in 1883 that single families who would not give up their fathers' faith went to Wischenka in Russia. In 1784, he says, part of the new converts fled to join them. The emigrants later moved on from Little Russia. Beck's preface says they went to the Crimea. His own note places their colony, Hutersthal, near the Sea of Azov, in the province of Taurida. In 1855, he says, the community stood under a grandson of the last bishop.

The two churches had been in touch before, by letter. In 1749 a Mennonite preacher, Franz Simon Sporer, wrote to the Brethren at Levar in Hungary. In 1757 another, Peter Weber, wrote to Zacharias Walter. He offered to send Menno's books.

set.longDescription:
Between 1793 and 1906 European and American missionary societies planted churches across India, West Africa, the Pacific and the China coast. And almost immediately those churches began to be run, staffed and spread by local Christians the societies had not planned for. Samuel Ajayi Crowther, enslaved as a boy in Yorubaland and freed by an anti-slavery patrol, translated the Bible into Yoruba and in 1864 became the first African Anglican bishop, only for the next generation of the same society to force him aside in 1890. In the Pacific it was hundreds of Polynesian teachers, not Europeans, who carried Christianity from island to island, often at the cost of their lives. In China the preacher Liang Fa wrote a tract in 1832 whose stray reading by Hong Xiuquan helped set the Taiping upheaval in motion, and the former opium addict known as Pastor Xi built a network of his own converts inland. What holds these four wings together is a single problem. Nearly everything written about them was written from the mission's side, and the native voices that do survive are what any honest telling has to be built on.

Liberia's settler church belongs to the West African wing. It came from America. Lott Cary was born a slave near Richmond, Virginia, about 1780, and the church there encouraged him to preach. About 1815 he helped rouse the Black Christians of Richmond to take an interest in Africa. The Richmond African Missionary Society that followed gave between one hundred and one hundred and fifty dollars to the African mission for several years. In 1821 Cary sailed for West Africa. In a letter from Free Town he wrote, 'Before we left the United States, we formed ourselves into a church'. On 16 August 1823 he wrote from Monrovia, 'Our little church has been wonderfully blessed of late.' He had baptized two the day before. Cary's words reach us through a biography by J. B. Taylor, a Richmond Baptist pastor, printed in 1837.
